Tesis para optar por el título de Licenciada en Ciencias Biológicas

Asignación filogenética proporcional de péptidos compartidos para la estimación de biomasa microbiana en metaproteómica

Autora: Nicole Fabre Barbero
Director: Dr. Lukas Käll
Codirector: Dr. Germán Rosano

Lugar de trabajo: Science for Life Laboratory (SciLifeLab), KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Estocolmo, Suecia (trabajo remoto)

Octubre de 2026

Resumen

La metaproteómica permite estimar la contribución de distintas especies a la biomasa total de una comunidad microbiana, pero dos prácticas habituales limitan estas estimaciones. Los péptidos compartidos entre organismos cercanos se descartan o se asignan sólo al ancestro común más cercano (LCA, por sus siglas en inglés) de esos organismos, y las identificaciones que no superan un umbral fijo de confianza se eliminan, mientras que las restantes se tratan como correctas. Esta tesis se pregunta si los péptidos compartidos pueden usarse para estimar la abundancia de cada especie, y si la probabilidad de que cada identificación sea correcta puede reemplazar al umbral de confianza. Se compararon cinco estrategias que asignan las intensidades de los péptidos sobre un árbol de especies, cada una de las cuales agrega un elemento a la anterior: descartar los péptidos compartidos, conservarlos en el LCA, repartirlos entre las cepas candidatas una vez o de forma iterativa con un algoritmo de esperanza-maximización (EM) y, por último, ponderar cada identificación por su probabilidad de ser correcta, 1 − PEP, donde PEP es la probabilidad de error posterior. Las estrategias se evaluaron en comunidades artificiales de unas 30 cepas de composición conocida, procesadas sin filtro de tasa de falsos descubrimientos, y en comunidades simuladas en las que se variaron la proporción de péptidos compartidos y la tasa de identificaciones falsas. Conservar los péptidos compartidos en el LCA dio totales correctos para los clados, mientras que descartarlos subestimó fuertemente los clados formados por cepas emparentadas. A nivel de especie, solo el reparto de la señal compartida corrigió las cepas con señal mayormente compartida, cuyo error pasó de decenas de veces a menos de tres veces. Usar todas las identificaciones ponderadas por 1 − PEP fue significativamente más exacto que aplicar un umbral estricto en dos de los tres diseños de la comunidad, principalmente porque recuperó las cepas poco abundantes, a costa de un leve aumento de la señal falsa en las cepas ausentes. En las simulaciones, cuando la confianza de las identificaciones correctas dependía de su intensidad, como en los datos reales, esta ponderación redujo el error de las especies raras en casi todas las comunidades, mientras que usar todas las identificaciones sin ponderarlas aumentó la señal falsa. Estos resultados muestran que los péptidos compartidos deben conservarse en el árbol y repartirse entre las especies, y que la confianza de cada identificación puede reemplazar a un umbral fijo al estimar abundancias.

Palabras clave: metaproteómica, péptidos compartidos, ancestro común más cercano, probabilidad de error posterior, estimación de biomasa, comunidad artificial.

Abstract

Proportional phylogenetic allocation of shared peptides for microbial biomass estimation in metaproteomics

Metaproteomics allows for the estimation of the contribution of different species to the total biomass of a microbial community, but two common practices limit these estimates. Peptides shared by closely related organisms are either discarded or assigned only to the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of those organisms, and identifications below a fixed confidence threshold are removed, while the remaining ones are treated as correct. This thesis asks whether shared peptides can be used to estimate the abundance of each species, and whether the probability that each identification is correct can replace the confidence threshold. Five strategies that allocate peptide intensities on a species tree were compared, each adding one element to the previous one: discarding shared peptides, keeping them at the LCA, splitting them among the candidate strains once or iteratively with an expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm and, finally, weighting every identification by its probability of being correct, 1 − PEP, where PEP is the posterior error probability. The strategies were evaluated on mock communities of about 30 strains with known composition, processed without false discovery rate filtering, and on simulated communities in which the proportion of shared peptides and the rate of false identifications were varied. Keeping shared peptides at the LCA gave correct totals for the clades, whereas discarding them strongly underestimated the clades formed by closely related strains. At the species level, only splitting the shared signal corrected the strains whose signal is mostly shared, reducing their error from more than tenfold to less than threefold. Using every identification weighted by 1 − PEP was significantly more accurate than a strict threshold in two of the three community designs, mainly because it recovered low-abundance strains, at the cost of a small increase in false signal on absent strains. In the simulations, when the confidence of correct identifications depended on their intensity, as in the real data, this weighting reduced the error of rare species in almost every community, whereas using every identification without weights increased the false signal. These results show that shared peptides should be kept on the tree and split among species, and that the confidence of each identification can replace a fixed threshold when estimating abundances.

Keywords: metaproteomics, shared peptides, lowest common ancestor, posterior error probability, biomass estimation, mock community.

1. Introduction

1.1 Microbiomes and metaproteomics

The microbiome is defined as a characteristic microbial community occupying a reasonably well-defined habitat with distinct physico-chemical properties. The term refers not only to the microorganisms involved but also to their theatre of activity, which results in the formation of specific ecological niches. The term “microbiota” refers to the living organisms in a given microbiome (Berg et al., 2020). Microbiomes are made up of bacteria, archaea, bacteriophages and other viruses, fungi and protozoa, and their taxonomic composition is highly diverse. In most cases they are highly structured in both membership and function, and there is growing evidence of their importance in virtually all processes of the biosphere (Van Den Bossche et al., 2025). Therefore, to understand a microbiome and its interaction with its environment or host, it is necessary to know which organisms make it up and in what proportions, as well as what functions they perform.

The term “metaproteomics” was first used for the large-scale characterization of the entire protein complement of environmental microbiota at a given point in time (Wilmes and Bond, 2004). Mass spectrometry-based metaproteomics determines the taxonomic composition of microbiomes while offering insights into the relative biomass of each taxon, because it reflects the protein content of each taxon within a sample. It is a powerful, high-throughput method for studying microbiomes that enables the direct identification and quantification of biological functions, whereas metagenomics and metatranscriptomics provide insight only into potential functions and gene expression (Alves et al., 2025). Metaproteomics comprehensively analyzes the proteins expressed within a microbiome, quantifying their abundance and characterizing their modifications, interactions and localizations. As the primary catalytic and structural elements of the cell, proteins directly reflect the microbiome’s phenotype (Van Den Bossche et al., 2025).

1.2 Proteins as a measure of biomass

Metaproteomics enables the study of the functions of environmental microbiomes, and also of their composition. Since proteins make up a large part of the cellular dry mass (about 55 % in Escherichia coli, Neidhardt and Umbarger, 1996), they are excellent estimators of microbial biomass (Kleiner et al., 2017). Using mock communities of known composition, Kleiner et al. (2017) showed that metaproteomic estimates of the proteinaceous biomass of each species agree better with the true community composition than estimates from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing or from metagenomics. Consequently, protein abundance provides a more direct proxy for biomass than gene-centric approaches. However, their study also identified the main difficulties of the approach: abundances of species present in low amounts are underestimated, quantification depends on how proteins are inferred from peptides, and closely related strains are hard to distinguish (Kleiner et al., 2017).

1.3 From spectra to organisms: identification and its uncertainty

In shotgun proteomics, the most common proteomic method, proteins are digested into peptides, which are separated by liquid chromatography and analysed by tandem mass spectrometry. In each measurement cycle the instrument first records the intact peptide ions (the MS1 spectrum); the intensity of a peptide in this spectrum is the signal used to quantify it. It then isolates and fragments selected ions and records their fragment spectra (MS2 spectra), which are used to identify them (Van Den Bossche et al., 2025). The peptides are identified by comparing the measured fragment spectra with the theoretical spectra of peptides from a protein sequence database, and proteins are then inferred from the identified peptides (Kleiner et al., 2017; Nesvizhskii and Aebersold, 2005). In metaproteomics the database contains the proteomes of many organisms, so the same steps also determine which organisms each peptide can come from.

Every peptide-spectrum match (PSM) is uncertain. Its reliability is usually controlled with a target–decoy search, in which the spectra are also searched against reversed or shuffled sequences that cannot be present, so that the number of decoy matches estimates the number of false target matches. From this comparison two quantities are derived: the false discovery rate (FDR) of a list of identifications above a score threshold, and the posterior error probability (PEP) of each individual PSM, that is, the probability that this particular match is wrong (The and Käll, 2019).

Accurate protein quantification is difficult in label-free shotgun proteomics because of the multiple sources of error in the method. Traditional pipelines control these errors through a series of filtering steps, typically keeping only identifications below 1 % FDR. However, the filtered results are then often treated as completely correct, ignoring the remaining uncertainty and discarding the evidence below the threshold. Such simplifications can compromise FDR control and lead to misleading interpretations. To address this problem, the Bayesian model Triqler quantifies and propagates multiple sources of error explicitly, from identification to differential abundance, and postpones filtering until the final step. Compared with traditional workflows, which make overconfident point estimates after heuristic filtering, Triqler achieves greater sensitivity and more accurate FDR control by relying on probability distributions (The and Käll, 2019). Triqler has also been shown to integrate with and outperform conventional methods for data-independent acquisition (Truong et al., 2023). This principle, that identification uncertainty should be propagated to the final result rather than filtered away, has not yet been applied to the estimation of organism abundances in metaproteomics.

1.4 The shared-peptide problem

Metaproteomics enables the characterization and quantification of proteins from microbial communities and can therefore be used to estimate the relative proteinaceous biomass contributed by different microorganisms (Hettich et al., 2012; Van Den Bossche et al., 2025). However, accurate biomass estimation remains challenging because quantitative information is initially obtained at the peptide level and must subsequently be assigned to proteins and taxa. Even in the proteomics of a single organism, the same peptide sequence can occur in several proteins. Deciding which proteins are present from this kind of evidence is known as the protein inference problem (Nesvizhskii and Aebersold, 2005). In metaproteomics the problem extends across organisms, because the same peptide can also occur in proteins of different species. Bacterial genomic homology generates considerable peptide redundancy through shared sequences among orthologous and paralogous proteins, limiting protein inference and taxonomic assignment, particularly among closely related species (Levi Mortera et al., 2019). Consequently, metaproteomic workflows commonly use protein grouping or taxonomic assignment strategies such as the lowest common ancestor (LCA) approach to handle shared peptide evidence. Although these methods help resolve ambiguous identifications, they can result in assignments at higher taxonomic levels and therefore limit the recovery of species-specific information (Alves et al., 2025).

In the LCA approach, introduced for metagenomic reads in MEGAN (Huson et al., 2007) and used for peptides by Unipept (Mesuere et al., 2016), a sequence that matches several taxa is assigned to their lowest common ancestor in the taxonomy, that is, to the most specific taxon that contains all of them. The rule is conservative, because a peptide is never assigned to a more specific taxon than its evidence supports. For quantification, however, it leaves a question open: when the signal of a shared peptide stays at the ancestor, how much of it belongs to each of the organisms below? Kleiner et al. (2017) took a different route and quantified species from proteins inferred with strict criteria based on protein-unique peptides, which provides high specificity but uses only part of the evidence.

These limitations are particularly relevant when metaproteomic measurements are used to estimate microbial biomass, because the way shared peptide signals are assigned directly affects the inferred abundance of individual taxa. For closely related strains that share most of their detectable peptides, a strategy based on unique peptides alone uses only a small fraction of the available signal, and their abundance can then be strongly underestimated.

1.5 Approaches that use shared peptides

Several methods already use shared peptides instead of discarding them, or take into account the confidence of the identifications, that is, how likely each identification is to be correct (Section 1.3), although each of them solves only part of the problem.

The LCA approach described in the previous section keeps the evidence of shared peptides, but leaves it at the common ancestor: it shows which taxa are present, but does not divide the signal among them. Pible et al. (2020) went a step further and showed that shared peptides carry quantitative information. For each organism they described how many of its spectra also match other taxa as a function of phylogenetic distance, a kind of “signature” of the organism, and they explained the spectral counts observed in a mixture as a combination of these signatures. With this approach, which they called phylopeptidomics, they estimated the proportions of two closely related pathogens in artificial mixtures.

The MiCId workflow (Alves et al., 2025; Alves et al., 2026) divides the signal of shared peptides directly. It first decides which taxa are present and then splits the MS1 intensity of each shared peptide among the identified taxa that contain it, using an expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm: the signal of each peptide is divided in proportion to the current abundance estimates of its taxa, the abundances are recomputed, and the two steps are repeated until they no longer change. MiCId estimates abundances at every taxonomic rank, so that an internal node of the tree can keep part of the signal. On synthetic communities, this redistribution estimated biomass more accurately than Unipept and MetaGOmics (Alves et al., 2025). The same principle is used in other fields: in RNA-seq, to divide reads that map to several transcripts (Li and Dewey, 2011), and in metagenomics, where Bracken redistributes to the species the reads that Kraken could only classify at a higher rank (Lu et al., 2017; Wood and Salzberg, 2014).

The Peptonizer2000 (Holstein et al., 2026) is the method that comes closest to using identification confidence. It combines the score of every peptide, as reported by the search engine, with the peptide-to-taxon links of Unipept in a graphical model, and reports for each taxon the probability that it is present in the sample. Because it takes the uncertainty of each peptide into account, it can use less confident identifications: in a search against a very large reference database, changing the FDR threshold from 1 % to 5 % improved its results slightly, whereas those of Unipept became worse (Holstein et al., 2026). However, this method estimates which taxa are present, not their abundance.

In all the methods that estimate abundance, identification confidence is handled with a threshold: only the identifications of a list whose FDR does not exceed 1 % are accepted (Section 1.3), and all accepted identifications are then treated as correct. The Peptonizer2000 is the exception, but it uses confidence only to decide which taxa are present. No method uses the probability that each identification is correct, its PEP, to weight its contribution to the abundance of organisms. Nor have the ingredients that these methods combine (keeping shared peptides on the tree, splitting them among organisms, iterating the split and accounting for identification error) been tested one at a time against a known composition, so it is not known how much each of them contributes. In this work these components are evaluated separately, and the PEP is proposed as a weight for abundance.

1.6 Benchmarking with communities of known composition

Although current quantification strategies can provide useful estimates of microbial abundance, their accuracy and reliability still require systematic benchmarking, that is, testing on data for which the correct answer is known, under controlled conditions (Van Den Bossche et al., 2025). In this context, mock microbial communities with defined compositions provide a controlled framework for evaluating whether metaproteomic measurements accurately recover known biomass contributions. Such benchmark datasets are therefore important for assessing the accuracy, reproducibility and reliability of quantitative approaches and for developing improved methods for metaproteomic biomass estimation (Van Den Bossche et al., 2025).

The mock communities of Kleiner et al. (2017) are well suited for this purpose: about 30 strains of bacteria, archaea, a eukaryote and bacteriophages were combined in three designs with known protein amounts, including closely related strain pairs that share most of their peptides and strains deliberately left out of some designs.

Following this need for systematic benchmarking, the present study develops a method that places peptide abundances on a species tree and evaluates it on mock microbial communities of known composition, to assess the accuracy of species-level biomass estimation from metaproteomic data. By comparing estimated abundances with experimentally defined biomass contributions, this framework provides a controlled setting to evaluate how shared peptide information, and the uncertainty of each identification, can be used for quantitative taxonomic assignment.

2. Objectives and hypotheses

General objective

To develop and evaluate a method that estimates the abundance of microbial species and strains from metaproteomic peptide data by allocating the signal of each peptide on a species tree, explicitly addressing peptides shared between organisms and the uncertainty of each peptide identification.

Research question

How should peptides shared between organisms, and the confidence of each identification, be used to estimate the abundance of the species in a microbial community?

Specific objectives

  1. To implement the allocation of quantMS peptide intensities onto a species tree, with five strategies of increasing complexity: Unique, Rigid LCA, Proportional, EM and EM + PEP.
  2. To evaluate these strategies on the mock communities of Kleiner et al. (2017) against their known composition, at the level of species and of internal tree nodes.
  3. To determine, with simulated communities, under which conditions of shared-peptide proportion and false-identification rate each component improves the estimates, and whether part of the signal should be assigned to internal nodes of the tree.

Hypotheses

H1. When quantitative evidence maps to multiple closely related species, assigning this evidence to their most specific shared taxonomic level (their lowest common ancestor) yields more complete and reliable abundance estimates than excluding it, and should be preferred in species-resolved analyses.

H2. Weighting each identification by its probability of being correct (1 − PEP), instead of applying a fixed confidence threshold, gives more accurate abundance estimates, especially for organisms present at low abundance.

3. Materials and Methods

3.1 Dataset

The mock microbial communities of Kleiner et al. (2017) (PRIDE PXD006118) were used because their composition is known. The communities contain 30 strains (bacteria, archaea, one eukaryote and five bacteriophages), prepared in three designs:

  • Constant (C): equal cell number per strain.
  • Protein (P): equal protein amount per strain.
  • Uneven (U): per-strain amounts spanning roughly three orders of magnitude.

Four strains (DVH, Ne1, Nu1, Nm1) were not added in designs C and P. These eight strain–design combinations are true negatives: any abundance assigned to them is false signal.

The 460 min one-dimensional liquid chromatography runs were used: 3 designs × 4 biological replicates × 2 technical replicates = 24 RAW files, acquired on a Q Exactive Plus in a single batch and in a randomized block design. The technical replicates are two injections of the same sample. The biological replicates are four mixtures assembled separately from frozen aliquots of a single culture of each organism (Kleiner et al., 2017), so they reflect the variation of assembly, preparation and measurement, not the biological variation between communities.

The expected proportion of strain s in design c (es,c) is its added protein amount divided by the total protein added in that design, so that Σs es,c = 1. Strains are referred to by the codes of Kleiner et al. (2017).

3.2 Identification and error probabilities

RAW files were processed with quantMS 1.7.0 (Dai et al., 2024), an automated OpenMS-based pipeline that takes raw data to identified and quantified peptides. For label-free DDA data, quantMS converts the RAW files to mzML, adds decoy sequences to the database, searches the spectra with Comet, rescores the identifications with Percolator, filters by FDR and quantifies the MS1 intensity of each peptide. Of its outputs, only the Triqler input table was used, which has one row per peptide (with its charge and modifications) in each run, with the score of its best PSM (parameters in Supplementary material II). Hereafter, each row of this table (a peptide with its charge in one run) is called an identification.

This workflow is configured with an SDRF-Proteomics file (Dai et al., 2021), a standard format recommended by PRIDE that describes in a table each RAW file with its sample, design, replicates and search parameters. Because the experiment of Kleiner et al. (2017) predates this format, the file was built manually from the original description (Supplementary material I).

Spectra were searched against the protein database published by Kleiner et al. (2017), which contains the proteomes of the community strains and common laboratory contaminant proteins (cRAP). quantMS added reversed decoy sequences to estimate the FDR (target–decoy search). Trypsin, cysteine carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification, methionine oxidation and protein N-terminal acetylation as variable modifications, and tolerances of 10 ppm for the precursor and 0.1 Da for the fragments were used. For each identification, the table includes the run, the MS1 intensity, the peptide sequence, the proteins that contain it, whether it is a decoy, and an identification score equal to 1 − PEP, where the PEP is the posterior error probability assigned by Percolator at the level of individual spectra; the score ranges from 0 to 1 and is higher for more reliable identifications.

The search was exported in two ways from the same RAW files:

  • Standard table: with the default quantMS filter (FDR ≤ 1 %). It contains 554,725 identifications, almost all of high confidence (minimum score 0.900).
  • Unfiltered table: with every quantMS FDR filter disabled. It contains about 2.96 million identifications, targets and decoys, with scores across the full 0–1 range.

Unless stated otherwise, results come from the unfiltered table.

PEP estimation. Percolator computes the PEP of each spectrum separately, but each row of the table summarises a peptide in one run. These probabilities cannot be transferred directly from one level to the other (Granholm et al., 2013): a peptide present in the sample is usually identified by several spectra, whereas incorrect identifications are spread over many different peptides, so that reducing spectra to peptides increases the fraction of incorrect identifications. Percolator’s PEP therefore underestimates the errors at the level of the table rows. In the unfiltered table, for example, the target identifications with score ≥ 0.99 add up to a Percolator PEP equivalent to about 250 incorrect identifications, whereas there are 3,186 decoys in that range. Following the procedure recommended at the peptide level, which is to reduce first and estimate afterwards (Granholm et al., 2013), the PEP of each identification was re-estimated from the decoys of the table itself with equation (1):

PEP(s)=h(s)1−h(s)(1) \mathrm{PEP}(s) = \frac{h(s)}{1 - h(s)} \qquad\qquad (1)

where s is the identification score and h(s) is the probability that an identification with that score is a decoy, fitted by isotonic regression over all identifications (Käll et al., 2008). Because each spectrum is assigned to a single sequence, target or decoy, and the database contains as many decoy as target sequences, each decoy stands for approximately one incorrect target identification; h/(1 − h) thus estimates the fraction of target identifications with that score that are incorrect. In the standard table the filter leaves very few decoys (0.2 %) and removes low-score identifications, so this fit is not possible; there, Percolator’s PEP (1 − score) was used directly. Because that PEP is at the spectrum level and underestimates peptide-level errors, the results of the standard table are considered only a sensitivity analysis.

Identifications used by each arm. Decoys and identifications that match no community strain (contaminants) were removed. Arms 1–4 (Unique, Rigid LCA, Proportional and EM) use only identifications with PEP < 0.01. Arm 5 (EM + PEP) uses all remaining identifications, with no threshold.

3.3 Allocation arms

The five allocation strategies are referred to as arms. The candidate set Cᵢ of identification i is the set of strains whose proteome contains the identified peptide. The identification is unique if |Cᵢ| = 1 and shared otherwise. Sharing strains are those that obtain at least half of their signal from shared peptides (Table S2). The species tree was built from NCBI Taxonomy (Schoch et al., 2020) with ete3 (Huerta-Cepas et al., 2016), with each strain as its own leaf (Table S1).

All arms work within each run and estimate πₛ, the fraction of the run’s peptide signal that belongs to strain s (Σₛ πₛ = 1). This fraction is used directly as the estimate of the strain’s protein biomass proportion, without a protein inference step. Each arm adds a single component to the previous one, so the difference between two consecutive arms can be attributed to that component.

Arms 3–5 split each shared identification among its candidate strains in proportion to the estimated abundance of each, with the rule of equation (2):

πs(t+1)∝∑i:s∈Ciwiπs(t)∑s′∈Ciπs′(t)(2) \pi_s^{(t+1)} \propto \sum_{i \,:\, s \in C_i} w_i \, \frac{\pi_s^{(t)}}{\sum_{s' \in C_i} \pi_{s'}^{(t)}} \qquad\qquad (2)

where πₛ⁽ᵗ⁾ is the proportion of strain s at step t, wᵢ is the weight of identification i, and the sum runs over the identifications whose candidate set includes s. That is, the weight of each identification is split among its candidates in proportion to their current abundance, and the proportions are recomputed from those splits. Applied once, starting from the unique signal, this rule is the proportional split. Applied repeatedly until the proportions stop changing, it is the expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm, which reaches the proportions that best explain the observed intensities (maximum likelihood) if each identification comes from exactly one of its candidates. It is the same estimator used in RNA-seq for reads that map to several transcripts (Li and Dewey, 2011), and MiCId also uses an EM algorithm (Alves et al., 2026).

  1. Unique. Only unique identifications are used; πₛ is the MS1 intensity of the unique identifications of strain s divided by that of all unique identifications.
  2. Rigid LCA. Each identification is assigned to the LCA of its candidate set and its intensity is summed at that node. Shared signal stays at internal nodes, so each leaf receives only its unique identifications. Because shared signal reaches no leaf, in this arm the leaf proportions add up to less than 1; each is expressed as a fraction of the total signal of the run.
  3. Proportional. A single step of equation (2) with wᵢ = Iᵢ, the MS1 intensity of the identification, started from the Unique estimate: each shared identification is split in proportion to the unique signal of its candidates.
  4. EM. Equation (2) with wᵢ = Iᵢ, iterated from a uniform π to convergence (total change below 10⁻¹⁰), so that the result does not depend on the Unique estimate.
  5. EM + PEP. As EM, but with all identifications and the weight of equation (3):

wi=Ii(1−pi)(3) w_i = I_i \, (1 - p_i) \qquad\qquad (3)

where pᵢ is the PEP of identification i. An identification that is probably false contributes little intensity and cannot create much signal on an absent strain.

Figure 1 shows how each arm treats the same evidence in a simplified example.

Figure 1. The five arms applied to a toy community with two related strains (A and B, same species), an unrelated strain (C) and an absent strain (D). Top: each identification, with its MS1 intensity and PEP, linked to the strains whose proteomes contain it. Bottom: where each arm places the shared peptide pep3 (mini-trees) and the intensity each strain receives (bars). EM + PEP recovers evidence for C (pep5) but also lets a little false signal reach D (pep6).

3.4 Evaluation and statistical analysis

Per-strain estimate. Run proportions were averaged over the two technical replicates and then over the four biological replicates of each design, giving one estimate ms,c per strain and design. The unit of analysis is the strain, not the run: the 24 runs are not independent, because technical replicates share a sample and all replicates of a design share the same expected values, and treating them as independent observations would be pseudoreplication. Thus n = 26 present strains in Constant and Protein and n = 30 in Uneven.

Tree nodes. The primary evaluation uses the leaves, because internal nodes are sums of leaves and add no independent observations. The abundance of an internal node is the sum of its leaves or, for Rigid LCA, the intensity assigned at or below that node. The 35 internal nodes with at least two community strains were compared descriptively with the summed expected proportions of their strains.

Metrics. The error of each present strain was measured as the x-fold deviation from its expected proportion: the ratio m/e or its inverse, whichever is larger than 1. A perfect estimate has a deviation of 1, and one at double or half the true value, a deviation of 2. It is an adaptation of the metric of Kleiner et al. (2017), in which a perfect estimate is 0, undetected species are excluded and the mean is reported. Here, estimates equal to zero were imputed with a minimum value of 10⁻⁶ (0.0001 %), so that all arms are evaluated on the same strains and an undetected strain counts as an error, and the median is reported, because a few strains with very large errors would dominate the mean. For each arm and design, the median x-fold deviation and its interquartile range (IQR) are reported; the L1 distance, Σₛ |mₛ − eₛ|, which measures the total misplaced proportion (0 = perfect, 2 = completely different); and the absent leakage, the percentage of the estimate assigned to DVH, Ne1, Nu1 and Nm1 in Constant and Protein.

Planned comparisons. Four paired comparisons were planned, one per added component: Unique → Proportional and Rigid LCA → Proportional (splitting the shared signal), Proportional → EM (iterating the split from a starting point that does not depend on the unique peptides) and EM → EM + PEP (weighting instead of thresholding). For each comparison and design, a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test was applied to the log error of each strain, |log₁₀(m/e)|, with Holm correction across the three designs (α = 0.05). This test does not assume normality and, on the log scale, weighs a 2-fold error on a rare strain the same as on an abundant one. Confidence intervals for the difference in median error were computed from 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples of strains. Because a non-significant p is not enough to claim that two arms agree, the interval is reported for Proportional → EM. EM + PEP was considered non-inferior to EM when the upper bound of the interval was below 0.05 log₁₀ units, that is, when a typical strain was no more than 12 % further from its true value; this margin was fixed before the analysis.

Additional analyses. Besides the four comparisons, five analyses without a planned test were run:

  • PEP threshold: EM was repeated with seven PEP thresholds, from 0.001 to no threshold, with and without weighting, to check whether the conclusions depend on the chosen threshold.
  • Sharing strains: because the split can only change strains with shared signal, comparisons are also reported separately for sharing strains and for the rest. Because this group includes only four strains, the smallest possible Wilcoxon p is 0.125, so it is described without a statistical test.
  • Low-abundance strains (exploratory, not planned): the EM → EM + PEP comparison was repeated for strains with an expected proportion below 1 %.
  • Changes between designs: for each pair of designs, the observed fold change of each strain was compared with the expected one, using the Pearson correlation on the strains present in both designs, the Spearman correlation including the strains absent from one of them and, for the latter, whether the direction of change was recovered.
  • Standard table: the five arms were also applied to the standard table, to check whether the conclusions depend on the FDR filter.

3.5 Simulations

The Kleiner community has few shared peptides (8 % of intensity) and very few false identifications after a strict threshold. To evaluate the arms under other conditions, they were also applied to simulated communities.

Each simulated community has 30 species in 6 genera of 5, with abundances spanning about three orders of magnitude and 20 % absent species. For each of 8,000 peptides an origin species is drawn, and every other species also contains it with probability p if it is in the same genus and p/25 otherwise, so that peptides are shared more between related species. A peptide’s intensity is the sum of the abundances of the species that contain it, with noise. False identifications are added at a chosen rate, and scores and decoys are simulated so that the PEP is estimated with the same target–decoy procedure as in the real data. As a reference, EM was also run on all identifications without weights (“EM, no threshold”). Four studies were run, with 20 independent communities per setting (Table 1).

Table 1. Simulation studies. Each study varies one factor and holds the others fixed.

Study What varies Fixed
A. Identification errors false identifications: 0, 2, 5 and 10 % 83 % unique peptides, as in the Kleiner community
B. Proportion of shared peptides from 83 % to 12 % unique peptides 5 % false identifications
C. Confidence depends on intensity as in A as in A, but the score of a correct identification increases with its intensity
D. Leaf-only vs all-rank allocation model, with and without PEP; 83 % and 30 % unique peptides 5 % false identifications

Study C was added because in the real data low-intensity identifications tend to have lower confidence. If the identifications of the unfiltered table are sorted by intensity and split into ten equal-sized groups, only 2 % of those in the lowest-intensity group pass PEP < 0.01, against 39 % of those in the highest-intensity group. Study D compares the model of this thesis, which assigns signal only to the leaves of the tree, with a model in which internal nodes can also keep part of the signal. It is inspired by MiCId, which estimates abundances at every taxonomic rank (Alves et al., 2025; Alves et al., 2026), but it is a simplified version of that idea: a single EM in which the candidates of each identification are all the nodes between its LCA and its strains, whereas MiCId repeats the EM separately at each rank. It was implemented in Python on the same evidence as the other arms; it is not the MiCId software.

In the simulations the communities are independent replicates, so the unit of analysis is the community. Arms were compared with a paired Wilcoxon test over the 20 communities, applied to the L1 distance and to the median log error, with Holm correction across the settings of each study.

3.6 Software and availability

All methods were implemented in Python 3 (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib) in the taxoshare library, developed in this work. The bootstrap and the simulations use fixed random seeds, so every result is reproduced exactly. The mass spectrometry data are available in PRIDE (PXD006118). The code, the SDRF file, the steps to reproduce the analysis and the result tables are described in Supplementary material I and III. quantMS was run in Singularity containers (Kurtzer et al., 2017) on the Arrhenius cluster, provided by the National Academic Infrastructure for Supercomputing in Sweden (NAISS), funded by the Swedish Research Council.

4. Results

4.1 Splitting among strains

Among identifications with PEP < 0.01, 8 % of the intensity maps to more than one strain, and 99 % of that shared signal belongs to three strain pairs: 841 + VF, 137 + 259 and K12 + LT2. Only four strains obtain more than half of their signal from shared peptides: 841, VF, 137 and 259 (Table S2).

Splitting the shared signal corrected these four strains and left the rest practically unchanged (Figure 2). Their median error was 15 to 45-fold with Unique and with Rigid LCA, depending on the design, and 1.6 to 2.7-fold with Proportional; all four improved in all three designs. In the other strains the change was not significant (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon, p ≥ 0.09). As a result, over all strains the difference between Unique and Proportional was not significant in any design, although the largest errors disappeared. EM gave the same estimates as Proportional in every design (difference in median error below 0.001 log₁₀ units). The metrics per arm are in Table S3 and the comparisons in Table S5.

Figure 2. X-fold deviation of the four sharing strains (coloured lines) and of the other strains (median and interquartile range, grey) under each arm. A deviation of 1 is a perfect estimate. Per-strain values are in Table S4.

4.2 Internal nodes

At the internal nodes of the tree, Rigid LCA, Proportional and EM gave the same values, and the two clades formed by strain pairs were close to their expected value (Figure 3). Unique, in contrast, underestimated the Rhizobium clade 9 to 12-fold and the Staphylococcus aureus clade 17 to 109-fold. The Enterobacteriaceae clade was underestimated about 1.7-fold in Uneven by every arm, because LT2, the most abundant strain in that design, was itself underestimated. All node values are in Table S6.

Figure 3. Estimated abundance of the three clades that carry almost all of the shared signal, compared with the expected value. At these nodes, Rigid LCA, Proportional and EM give the same value.

4.3 PEP weighting

At PEP thresholds up to 0.25, weighting or not by 1 − PEP gave the same result (Figure 4). The difference appeared when all identifications were used: without weighting, absent leakage rose above 6 %, and with weighting it stayed at about 1 %.

Figure 4. Effect of the PEP threshold on EM, without weighting (green) and with 1 − PEP weighting (red). “None” means that every identification was used (values in Table S7). Uneven has no absent strains, so the lower right panel stays at zero.

EM + PEP without a threshold was significantly more accurate than EM with a strict threshold in Protein and Uneven, and non-inferior in both; in Constant there was no significant difference and non-inferiority could not be established (Table 2). In exchange, absent leakage rose from 0.4–0.6 % to 0.9–1.0 %. With EM, about 80 % of that signal belongs to a single strain, Nm1, and comes from high-confidence identifications. With EM + PEP, Nm1 is still the strain that receives the most signal (about half), and the rest is spread over the other three (Table S8).

Table 2. EM with a strict threshold (PEP < 0.01) versus EM + PEP without a threshold. Significant differences in bold (paired Wilcoxon with Holm correction).

Design Median x-fold, EM Median x-fold, EM + PEP p Absent leakage, EM → EM + PEP
Constant 1.50 1.56 0.57 0.59 % → 1.01 %
Protein 1.47 1.43 0.046 0.40 % → 0.87 %
Uneven 2.06 1.75 0.004 –

The gain was concentrated in low-abundance strains (Figure 5). In this exploratory analysis, 13 of the 16 strains in Uneven with an expected share below 1 % improved, and their median deviation fell from 3.5 to 1.8-fold (p = 0.002), whereas the 14 more abundant strains did not change significantly (p = 0.39). The result held when the four strains absent from the other designs were excluded (9 of 12 improved; p = 0.010). These p-values are uncorrected.

Figure 5. X-fold deviation of each strain with thresholded EM (x-axis) and with EM + PEP (y-axis). Points below the diagonal improve with PEP weighting; strains with an expected share below 1 % are shown in orange.

On the standard table (FDR ≤ 1 %), the conclusions for arms 1–4 were the same, and EM + PEP did not differ from EM (p ≥ 0.13).

4.4 Changes between designs

Table 3 compares, for each pair of designs, the observed fold change of each strain with the expected one. The thresholded arms recovered the changes similarly, and EM + PEP gave the best agreement in the two contrasts involving Uneven. The direction of change of the four strains absent from Constant and Protein was recovered poorly by every arm, because their estimated abundance in Uneven (0.02–0.11 % with EM) is of the same order as the false signal they receive in the designs where they are absent.

4.5 Simulations

Figure 6 summarises the results on the simulated communities (Table 1).

Figure 6. Performance of the arms on the simulated communities (mean of 20 communities per point; bars: standard error). Rigid LCA is not shown because its error is off the scale. Panels A, B and C correspond to the studies in Table 1 (values in Tables S10 and S11).

When the proportion of shared peptides was that of the mock community, Proportional and Unique gave similar results. As that proportion increased, Unique degraded and Proportional did not: with 12 % unique peptides, Proportional was better in all 20 communities (p < 0.0001). Iterating the split improved the result only at that extreme (EM better in 17 of 20 communities; p = 0.0008) (study B).

Using all identifications without weights degraded the estimates as false identifications increased, whereas with PEP weighting the same input gave results similar to the strict threshold (study A). When the confidence of a correct identification did not depend on its intensity, the strict threshold removed almost all false identifications and few correct ones, and EM + PEP did not beat it: the L1 distance was similar and the median species error was slightly higher with 5 and 10 % false identifications (p ≤ 0.025). With many shared peptides (study B, 12 % unique peptides), EM + PEP was also somewhat worse than EM (p = 0.0003). When confidence depended on intensity (study C), the threshold discarded 21 to 35 % of correct identifications, mostly from low-abundance species. There, EM + PEP reduced the error of rare species from 2.0–2.4 to 1.2-fold, and the median error was lower in 19 or 20 of the 20 communities (p ≤ 0.0001).

In study D, the leaf-only and all-rank models gave the same genus totals. When 83 % of the peptides were unique, both models also agreed at the leaves. With 30 % unique peptides, however, the all-rank model kept part of the signal at the genus nodes, and the median species deviation increased from 1.07 to 3.4-fold. This error was larger in all 20 communities (p < 0.0001). PEP weighting had the same effect on both models, with no significant difference from EM (Table S12).

5. Discussion and Conclusions

The results show that shared peptides should not be discarded, since on the tree they give correct clade totals and, split among strains, they correct the strains that depend on them. Iterating the split improved the estimates only when many peptides were shared, and weighting each identification by its probability of being correct was able to replace the confidence threshold, especially for low-abundance organisms.

5.1 Shared peptides (H1)

The first hypothesis proposed that assigning shared evidence to the lowest common ancestor of the species that contain it gives more complete estimates than excluding it. At the clade level, the results support it: discarding shared peptides removed almost all of the signal of the clades formed by related strains, whereas keeping them at the LCA placed those clades close to their true value. At the species level, however, the hypothesis needs to be refined. Leaving the signal at the ancestor does not change any leaf, so strains whose signal is almost entirely shared remain as underestimated as if that signal had been discarded. Only splitting it among the candidate strains corrects them. Keeping the signal on the tree makes it possible to estimate how much belongs to each clade, and the split makes it possible to distribute that amount among the strains that form it. Because a shared peptide is only split among strains below its LCA, the split never changes the clade total.

This distinction is important because the LCA is the usual way of handling shared evidence in metaproteomics. MEGAN (Huson et al., 2007) and Unipept (Mesuere et al., 2016) assign each ambiguous sequence to the LCA of its matches, and most pipelines adopt this criterion (Alves et al., 2025; Holstein et al., 2026). For identification the LCA is a sound rule, because it never claims more resolution than the evidence allows. For species-level quantification, however, it is incomplete, since an explicit decision on how to divide the ancestor’s signal is needed.

The split separated strains that identification-based methods cannot tell apart. The two Rhizobium strains of the mock community share almost all their peptides. Kleiner et al. (2017) could not resolve them with protein inference, and Peptonizer2000 reported two Rhizobium species as present in the same community because the detected peptides do not distinguish them (Holstein et al., 2026). In the community analysed, the few unique peptides of each strain were enough to anchor the split and correct the estimate of both in all three designs.

The idea of using shared peptides has precedents. Pible et al. (2020) showed that the pattern of peptides shared between organisms carries quantitative information, and in metagenomics Bracken redistributes to species the reads that Kraken could only assign to a higher rank (Lu et al., 2017; Wood and Salzberg, 2014), analogous to the Proportional arm. What this thesis adds is an evaluation of each of these components separately against a known composition.

In the mock community the effect was concentrated in four strains, because shared peptides carry only 8 % of the intensity and almost all of them belong to three strain pairs. Most strains therefore changed little and the test over all strains was not significant, although the largest errors disappeared. The simulations show that the effect grows with the proportion of shared peptides, and real communities with many related strains, such as the human gut, can be expected to be closer to that scenario.

Iterating the split with EM changed nothing in the mock community, because with few shared peptides the Proportional starting point is already close to the solution. In the simulations, EM was better only with many shared peptides. Since it has no practical cost and does not require every strain to have unique peptides, it is a reasonable default. This estimator is the one used in RNA-seq for reads that map to several transcripts (Li and Dewey, 2011) and the one used by MiCId in metaproteomics (Alves et al., 2025; Alves et al., 2026), which also lets internal nodes keep part of the signal. In the simulations, this all-rank model gave the same clade totals as the leaf-only model, but with many shared peptides it kept signal at internal nodes and lost resolution at the species level. This result corresponds to a complete database. When the sample contains organisms missing from the database, whose peptides can only be explained by a higher rank, signal at internal nodes may be useful (Section 5.3).

5.2 PEP weighting (H2)

Metaproteomic allocation methods, including those that split shared peptides, quantify only the identifications that pass a threshold and treat them as correct. Peptonizer2000 (Holstein et al., 2026) does use the confidence of each peptide, but to decide which taxa are present, not how much of each there is. No published method was found that uses the PEP of each identification to weight its contribution to the abundance of organisms. The idea follows the principle of Triqler (The and Käll, 2019): identification uncertainty is propagated into quantification instead of being removed with a filter. With weights, uncertain identifications contribute less signal instead of being removed, and a threshold is no longer needed. Because the weight acts on the evidence and not on the allocation model, it can be added to any allocation method; in the simulations it had the same effect on the leaf-only and the all-rank models.

The second hypothesis proposed that this weighting gives more accurate abundances than a threshold, in particular for low-abundance organisms. The results support it in two of the three designs, and show that it is the weights that make it safe to use every identification: without them, false signal on absent strains rose tenfold. The gain was concentrated in low-abundance strains. This can be explained because, in these data, the confidence of an identification depends on its intensity, so a strict threshold discards proportionally more evidence from rare organisms and underestimates them. Kleiner et al. (2017) observed the same bias, since all their approaches underestimated low-abundance species. The simulations reproduce the mechanism: when confidence did not depend on intensity the threshold was enough, and when it did, weighting clearly reduced the error of rare species. A benefit is therefore expected when, as in the real data, rare organisms are identified with lower confidence. Although the analysis by abundance was not planned and is reported as exploratory, the result held when the strains absent from other designs were excluded and agreed with the simulation.

The cost of using every identification is a small increase in signal on absent strains. Weighting reduces how much a false identification contributes, but not which strain it is assigned to, so on a truly absent strain any positive weight produces some signal. This effect is inherent to the estimator and does not depend on the calibration of the PEP. Moreover, the strain that receives the most false signal, Nm1, receives it from high-confidence identifications, with or without weighting. For estimating the abundance of organisms that are present but rare, the balance between cost and benefit is favourable. For deciding whether an organism is present, abundance should be combined with a presence criterion, such as the taxon-level probability computed by Peptonizer2000.

The method requires calibrated PEPs. In this dataset, Percolator’s PEP, computed for individual spectra, underestimated false identifications at the peptide level, and had to be re-estimated from the decoys (Section 3.2). If the PEPs are not well calibrated, the weights act as a hidden threshold. Calibration should therefore be checked before applying the method, which is simple if the output keeps the decoys. For the same reason, on a table already filtered at 1 % FDR weighting does not change the results, because after the filter almost no uncertain identifications remain.

5.3 Limitations

The mock community is the only real dataset analysed; it has few shared peptides and only four strains could benefit from the split, too few for a statistical test. The simulations extend these conditions, but they only reproduce what was built into the simulator. In addition, the unit of analysis is the strain, which limits the observations to 26–30 per design and makes the conclusions depend on the strains of this community.

All strains were in the database. In real samples the database is often incomplete or contains relatives instead of the organisms present, and this choice strongly affects identification and taxonomic assignment (Tanca et al., 2013). In this same community, when one Rhizobium strain was removed from the database, part of its signal moved to its close relative (Kleiner et al., 2017). A model that splits among database strains will assign the signal of a missing organism to its relatives, and which model is preferable in that case was not evaluated.

Finally, no allocation method can separate organisms that share all their peptides, such as the three Salmonella strains that Kleiner et al. (2017) treated as one; for such groups the meaningful unit is the tree node. Errors in the measured quantity are not corrected either: the Enterobacteriaceae clade was underestimated by every arm because LT2 already was, a quantification problem that Kleiner et al. (2017) also described for the Uneven design.

5.4 Future work

  • Differential abundance at tree nodes. The original plan included a differential test between conditions at the tree nodes, which was not carried out. Methods such as treeclimbR (Huang et al., 2021), which choose the resolution of hierarchical hypotheses from the data, are a starting point. The tree should be used to place evidence rather than to share information between taxa, since smoothing along the phylogeny did not improve detection in microbiome studies (Bichat et al., 2020).
  • Integration into Triqler. The original plan proposed extending Triqler (The and Käll, 2019); during the work, the allocation problem turned out to be the central unsolved part. Integrating the allocation into Triqler would give a posterior distribution for the abundance of every node and a probabilistic differential test between conditions.
  • Better PEPs. Since the method depends on calibrated PEPs, rescoring tools such as MS2Rescore (Buur et al., 2024) could directly improve the abundances.
  • Real samples and incomplete databases. The next step is to apply the method to real communities, where shared peptides are much more frequent, and to evaluate what happens when the true organism is missing from the database, for example by removing proteomes from a mock community. That is also the setting in which to compare the leaf-only and all-rank models again.
  • Software. The allocation is implemented in the taxoshare library, which takes the quantMS output (Dai et al., 2024). Building the tree from the taxonomy of the search database would make the workflow fully automatic for any dataset described with SDRF (Dai et al., 2021).

5.5 Conclusions

  1. Shared peptides should be kept: placed at the lowest common ancestor, they give correct clade totals, whereas discarding them underestimates clades of related strains.
  2. For species abundances, the shared signal must also be split among the candidate strains; this corrects the strains that depend on shared peptides without changing the others.
  3. Iterating the split with EM gives the same result as a single step when few peptides are shared and improves it when many are.
  4. Weighting each identification by 1 − PEP can replace the confidence threshold: it was more accurate in two of the three designs, especially for low-abundance strains, at the cost of a small increase in signal on absent strains. This use of identification confidence for estimating abundance is the main contribution of this thesis.
  5. Weighting requires calibrated PEPs and an unfiltered search, and its benefit is largest when confidence depends on intensity, as in the real data.

Supplementary material

I. Code and reproducibility

The code, the SDRF file and the result tables are available in the GitHub repository https://github.com/nickyfabre/tesis-nicole-fabre-barbero. Paths are relative to the root of the repository.

Folder or file Content
taxoshare/ The library: taxonomy tree and LCA (tree.py), the five allocation arms, including EM (allocate.py), PEP estimation by target–decoy competition (pep.py), metrics, data loaders and the simulator (simulate.py)
tests/ Unit tests of the library
analysis/kleiner_benchmark/ Analysis of the mock communities: tree building, the five arms, statistics and figures
analysis/simulations/ Simulation studies A–D
files/ Input data: SDRF file, mock-community recipe and reference database (the large quantMS tables are not stored in the repository)

The results are reproduced with the following steps:

  1. Build the species tree from NCBI: analysis/kleiner_benchmark/build_taxonomy.py (writes taxonomy.json; manual name assignments in Table S1).
  2. Main analysis on the unfiltered quantMS table: analysis/kleiner_benchmark/thesis_benchmark.py --mode unfiltered.
  3. Sensitivity analysis on the standard 1 % FDR table: thesis_benchmark.py --mode filtered.
  4. Figures: Figures 1–3, thesis/make_figures_r5.py; the others, analysis/kleiner_benchmark/make_result_figures.py (Spanish versions: thesis/thesis es/make_figures_es.py).
  5. Simulations: analysis/simulations/run_simulations.py (about 10 minutes; fixed seeds).

II. quantMS parameters

quantMS 1.7.0 was run with --add_decoys true and --add_triqler_output true. For the unfiltered table, all FDR control points were set to 1.0: --fdr_threshold, --run_fdr_cutoff, --psm_level_fdr_cutoff and --protein_level_fdr_cutoff.

III. Supplementary tables

The supplementary tables are tab-separated files in the repository (Supplementary material I). Kleiner tables come from the unfiltered table; the same tables for the standard table (FDR ≤ 1 %) are in analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/filtered/.

Table Content File
S1 Strains whose name could not be matched to NCBI automatically, with the manual assignment and its source analysis/kleiner_benchmark/strain_names.tsv
S2 Fraction of each strain’s intensity that is shared with other strains, and classification as sharing strain analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/unfiltered/strain_sharing.tsv
S3 Headline metrics per arm and design: median x-fold deviation and IQR, L1 distance, absent leakage, log Pearson r, Spearman ρ, number of imputed estimates analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/unfiltered/summary.tsv
S4 Expected and estimated share, log error and x-fold deviation for every strain, arm and design analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/unfiltered/per_species.tsv
S5 Planned comparisons between arms: strata, medians, strains improved and worsened, Wilcoxon p, bootstrap confidence intervals, equivalence and non-inferiority analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/unfiltered/stats.tsv
S6 Estimated share at every node of the species tree, per arm and design analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/unfiltered/nodes.tsv
S7 Threshold analysis: EM at seven PEP thresholds, with and without 1 − PEP weighting analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/unfiltered/threshold_sweep.tsv
S8 Signal on the strains absent from Constant and Protein, per arm (mean and range over biological replicates) analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/unfiltered/absent.tsv
S9 Fold-change recovery between designs, per arm analysis/kleiner_benchmark/results/unfiltered/foldchange.tsv
S10 Simulation studies A–C: mean metrics per arm and setting analysis/simulations/results/summary.tsv
S11 Simulation studies A–C: paired tests between arms analysis/simulations/results/stats.tsv
